newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Go-it-alone Chiluba to slash Zambia spending.
newsitem.headline: Go-it-alone Chiluba to slash Zambia spending.

text.p: Zambia will drastically cut public spending in 1997 in response to aid cuts by Western governments unhappy with the country's political course, President Frederick Chiluba said on Friday.
In a tough, go-it-alone speech, he also signalled a clampdown on the media and election monitoring groups he described as unpatriotic.
"A major thrust of the budget will be living within our means by reducing, very drastically, the budget's dependence on external subventions," he told the first session of the new parliament.
Last year's state budget was 1,161.6 billion kwacha ($893 million), with 36 percent provided by foreign donors.

But Chiluba's controversial landslide re-election last November, with most opposition parties boycotting what they alleged was a rigged campaign, provoked cuts or the outright freezing of aid by the United States and other governments.
Several local and foreign monitoring groups said they did not consider the voting free or fair. About half of the country's 4.6 million electorate were excluded from the poll.

"It will be...necessary in the course of fiscal year 1997 and subsequent years to exercise strictest financial discipline and for all of us in the nation to tone down excessive demands which cannot be supported by the budget," Chiluba told MPs in Lusaka.
"It is important for the government to cede the dependency syndrome for outside assistance. No matter how significant and meaningful it is, it can be withdrawn at the whim of the benefactors."
Chiluba said local election monitors who questioned the legitimacy of the November poll were unpatriotic, and the government intended to introduce new legislation to regulate such "wilful" behaviour.
Chiluba said he planned new laws "which would make election monitoring teams and all non-governmental organisations accountable both to their members and to society".
The government also planned to introduce legislation establishing a media council to regulate the media, sections of which were irresponsible, he said.
Chiluba's ruling Movement for Multi-party Democracy dominates parliament, with 138 seats out of a total of 158 filled by its members. ($=1,290 kwacha)
